supports_model.mismatch_notes: SP-125 (Huzel & Huang) contains NO chamber-shoulder fillet radius, no symbol Rs or Rs,max, and no 0.8 factor anywhere in the thrust-chamber geometry text (grep of 'shoulder' hits only fatigue/seal contexts; 'fillet' only in the structural stress-concentration discussion). What the document DOES state, and what the registry's equation_ref ('SP-125 qualitative contraction factors') can legitimately point to, is qualitative: (a) any smooth, well-rounded convergent section has very low energy losses because subsonic velocities are low (PDF p. 98); (b) abrupt changes or discontinuities in the wall contour should be avoided (p. 98); (c) the contraction area ratio is optimized against seven listed factors - combustion performance/injector, gas-flow pressure drop, wall cooling, stability, weight, envelope, manufacturability (p. 97); (d) chamber total-pressure loss is a function of gamma and the contraction ratio via Rayleigh flow (pp. 14-15). The only NUMERIC radius guidance is for the THROAT arc (R = 0.5-1.5 Rt) plus a convergent half-angle range of 20-45 deg (p. 98); this is the throat-side upstream arc, not the cylinder-to-cone shoulder. The worked layouts (pp. 104-107) run a straight convergent cone from the cylindrical chamber to the throat arc with no shoulder fillet, and compute the convergent volume as a frustum cone. The only '0.8' in the neighbourhood is the 80-percent-bell nozzle length fraction (p. 107), unrelated to the shoulder. Figure 4-9 ('Elements of basic cylindrical combustion chamber') is not OCR-recoverable in the markdown, so a figure-labelled shoulder radius cannot be ruled out from the rendering, but no text refers to one. Net: the qualitative motivation is supported; the relation Rs = 0.8*Rs,max and the fill-fraction concept are repository policy, as the registry itself concedes, and should not be cited to SP-125.

supports_model.mismatch_notes: Hagemann et al. 1998 (Advanced Rocket Nozzles) is a qualitative review with no numbered equations. It does NOT state a quasi-one-dimensional attached-flow thrust-coefficient or nozzle momentum-balance relation anywhere; the 'Cf' half of the registry relation is absent. The paper only asserts that nonadapted exhaust flow induces a significant negative thrust contribution and that off-design over/underexpansion losses rise up to 15% (Table 1, Fig. 3). What the document DOES support is the 'explicit separation applicability' half and the equation_ref 'overexpanded nozzle flow and separation regimes': it defines over-/underexpanded off-design regimes, defines the critical pressure ratio p_cr = p_sep/p_p across the separation point, states that p_cr depends strongly on Mach number (slightly on Re) and also on wall temperature, gas composition and wall roughness, catalogs empirical separation-onset criteria (Summerfield, Schmucker, Keldysh empirical p_cr/p_p/p_w,e/p_amb relationships, Aerojet tabulated upper/lower separation ratios for conical vs bell nozzles, European p_sep/p_amb = f(local wall Mach number) criterion), and states that nozzle area ratios are chosen to avoid separation at nominal chamber pressure and that side-load prediction in the separated regime is uncertain/ongoing research. The registry validity_text ('attached flow only; separated-flow thrust must be withheld or separately modeled') is consistent with the paper's statements but is not phrased as a rule by the paper. The Cf momentum balance must be sourced elsewhere (the paper cites NASA SP-8120 as its Ref. 2).

supports_model.mismatch_notes: NASA SP-8089 (this document) contains no n-tau equation, no interaction-index or sensitive-time-lag values, and no sensitive-frequency formula. Its combustion-stability content (sec. 2.1.1.3, pp. 42-45; design criteria sec. 3.1.1.3, pp. 91-92) is qualitative design guidance: it classifies instability into chug (50-250 Hz), buzz (100-900 Hz), acoustic (>500 Hz) and hybrid (>500 Hz); gives a minimum delta-P_inj/P_ch of 5-20 percent (element-type dependent) to prevent chug; recommends estimating the oscillatory response of injector, feed system and combustion process and avoiding coincidence of fluid-system resonances with high combustion-process response; and defers all analytical modeling to references 57 (Harrje & Reardon, NASA SP-194), 62 (Priem), 63 (Smith et al., 'The Sensitive Time Lag Theory...', AFRPL-TR-67-314) and 64, stating that the models of refs. 63 and 64 'have been most widely used'. So the document supports the registry's framing (a frequency-band screen against combustion response, classical time-lag theory as the accepted tool) and its validity caveat (it is guidance, not a transfer-function or stability-margin prediction), but the n-tau relation itself must be sourced from ref. 63 or SP-194, not from this monograph.
